reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: A chronic, non-expandable lung caused by a fibrous visceral pleural peel that prevents the lung re-expanding to the chest wall
Results from a remote, now-quiescent pleural insult such as prior infection, haemothorax, or inflammation, in contrast to active lung entrapment where inflammation is ongoing
Produces a persistent, typically small to moderate pleural effusion that reaccumulates after drainage
The fluid is characteristically a transudate or borderline exudate formed by negative pleural pressure (ex vacuo effusion)
Pleural manometry shows a rapid, excessive fall in pleural pressure during fluid removal, and imaging after drainage reveals failure of the lung to fully expand
Repeated therapeutic thoracocentesis gives little lasting symptomatic benefit because the lung cannot expand
Definitive treatment when symptomatic is surgical decortication to release the visceral peel
reference.pathophysiology: Following a resolved pleural inflammatory process, a mature, relatively acellular fibrous membrane forms over the visceral pleura. This inelastic peel mechanically restrains the lung so that it cannot expand to fill the hemithorax. The persistently unexpanded lung creates an abnormally negative intrapleural pressure, which draws a transudative effusion into the space through an imbalance of hydrostatic forces rather than active inflammation. Because the driving mechanism is mechanical, the fluid recurs after drainage and the lung fails to re-expand, distinguishing established trapped lung from active entrapment where ongoing pleural inflammation is present.
additionalDifferentials: Active lung entrapment from ongoing pleural inflammation or malignancy
Malignant pleural effusion with visceral pleural involvement
additionalInvestigations: Chest radiograph before and after thoracocentesis to assess lung re-expansion
CT of the thorax to demonstrate visceral pleural thickening and exclude malignancy or endobronchial obstruction
Pleural fluid analysis, typically showing a transudate or borderline exudate
Pleural manometry demonstrating a steep pressure drop during fluid removal
Bronchoscopy where an endobronchial cause of non-expansion is suspected
redFlags: Features suggesting an underlying malignancy such as a bloody effusion or pleural nodularity
Signs of active or recurrent pleural infection
Development of a hydropneumothorax after attempted drainage
Progressive breathlessness with an enlarging pleural collection
reference.prognosis: Trapped lung itself is a stable, benign mechanical problem; symptomatic cases can improve after decortication if the underlying lung is healthy, whereas the outlook is dominated by any underlying malignant or infective cause when present.
pitfalls: Repeatedly draining the effusion without recognising that the lung cannot re-expand
Mislabelling a mechanical ex vacuo transudate as an unexplained exudate
Attempting pleurodesis when the lung will not appose the chest wall
Failing to distinguish quiescent trapped lung from active entrapment that needs treatment of ongoing disease
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
